essentialQuestion.source: Why does AI sometimes work well for some people and badly for others?
essentialQuestion.back: Why does AI sometimes work well for some groups of people but badly for others?

learningGoal.source: Explain how who is in the data, and other causes, can make an AI tool work worse for some groups of people, and why a gap in results shows a problem but not its cause.
learningGoal.back: Explain how who is in the data, and other causes, can make AI tools work worse for some groups, and why a gap in results says there is a problem but not its cause.

read.sections.0.text.source: At Riverbend Learning Centre, a team tested a voice typing tool. Teachers, older learners and the youngest learners each read the same 20 words. The tool was accurate for the teachers, with 19 words right. For the youngest learners, it got only 9 right. The gap shows that the tool works worse for young children. It does not show why. So the team looked for a cause. The tool had learned mostly from recordings of adults, so children's voices were new to it. Researchers have found this in real speech tools too. In a 2024 study, a widely used tool made several times as many mistakes with children's speech as with adults'. The researchers gave two reasons: there are far fewer recordings of children, and children's speech changes a lot as they grow.
read.sections.0.text.back: At the Riverbend learning centre a team tested a voice typing tool. Teachers, older learners and the youngest learners all read the same 20 words. The tool was accurate for the teachers, typing as many as 19 words correctly, but for the youngest learners it typed only 9 correctly. This gap shows the tool works worse with young children but does not say why, so the team set out to find the cause. The tool learned mostly from recordings of adults, so children's voices were new to it. Researchers have found this in real speech tools too. In a 2024 study a widely used tool made several times more mistakes with children's speech than with adults' voices. The researchers gave two reasons: there are far fewer recordings of children, and children's speech changes a lot as they grow.

read.sections.0.simpler.source: At Riverbend, a team tested a voice typing tool. Teachers and learners each read the same 20 words. The tool was accurate for the teachers. It got 19 right. Children's voices were new to it. In 2024, researchers found a real tool made many more mistakes with children. There are fewer recordings of children. And children's speech changes as they grow.

The tool learned mostly from adult voices, so children's voices were new to it. In 2024 researchers found that a real tool made many more mistakes with children. There are fewer recordings of children, and children's speech changes as they grow.

read.sections.1.text.source: When a tool works well for some groups of people and badly for others, we say it has a bias. One cause is the training data. Does it represent everyone who will use the tool? A famous collection of more than a million photos has been used to train many tools. About 45% of its photos were taken in the United States, and only about 2% in India. Researchers found that a tool trained on it was worse at naming things in photos from India or Pakistan, such as a bridegroom at a wedding. Nobody had to plan this for the result to be unfair.
read.sections.1.text.back: When a tool works well for some groups but badly for others, we say the tool has bias. One cause is the training data: does that data represent everyone who will use the tool? A famous photo collection of more than a million pictures was used to train many tools. About 45 percent of the photos were taken in the United States, and only about 2 percent in India. Researchers found that tools trained on this collection named things in pictures from India or Pakistan worse, such as a groom at a wedding. No one needs to have planned anything for the result to be unfair.

read.sections.1.simpler.source: Some tools work well for some people and badly for others. This is called bias. One cause is the training data. Does the data represent all the people who will use the tool? One big set of photos has trained many tools. Almost half its photos came from the United States. Very few came from India. A tool trained on it did worse with photos from India or Pakistan. Nobody had to plan this for it to be unfair.
read.sections.1.simpler.back: Some tools work well for some people but badly for others. We call this bias. One cause is the training data. Does the data represent everyone who will use the tool? One big photo collection was used to train many tools. Almost half the photos came from the United States. Very few came from India. Tools trained on this collection did worse with pictures from India or Pakistan. No one has to plan it; it can still be unfair.

read.sections.2.heading.source: The same gap can have different causes
read.sections.2.heading.back: The same gap can have different causes

read.sections.2.text.source: Two computer scientists described two made-up cases to explain this. In the first, a hospital tool missed more heart attacks in women than in men. The researcher added more records from women, and the tool improved. In the second, a hiring tool said women were less suitable for jobs. It had learned from people's past ratings of workers, and those ratings were unfair to women. Adding more of the same kind of data did not help. Both tools showed the same kind of gap, but the causes were different. Other causes include a tool's goal, its design, or using it in a place it wasn't made for. So people test a tool with many groups, look for the cause, and fix that.
read.sections.2.text.back: Two computer scientists tell two made-up cases to explain this. In the first case a hospital tool missed heart attacks in women more often than in men. The researchers added more records of women and the tool improved. In the second case a hiring tool said women were less suited to the job. The tool learned from scores people had given employees in the past, and those scores were unfair to women, so adding more of the same data did not help. The two tools show the same kind of gap but have different causes. Other causes also include the tool's goal, its design, or using it in places it was not built for. So people test tools with many groups, look for the cause, and then fix the cause.

watch.summary.source: This video explains why training data matters so much. A machine learning tool is only as good as the data it learns from. Data can come from many places. For example, a video site keeps track of what people watch, sometimes without them knowing. Then it uses that data to suggest more videos. In health care, experts label thousands of medical pictures, so a computer can learn to spot illness. But there is a problem. Suppose most of the X-ray pictures come from men. Then the tool may make more mistakes for women. People can put their own bias into training data without meaning to. So the video asks two questions about any training data. Is there enough of it? Does it include many kinds of people and situations?
watch.summary.back: This video explains why training data matters so much. A machine learning tool can only be as good as the data it learns from. Data can come from many places. For example, a video website collects data about what people watch, sometimes without them knowing, and uses it to recommend more videos. In health, experts label thousands of medical images so a computer learns to spot illness. But there is a problem. Suppose most X-rays come from men; the tool may make more mistakes with women. People may put their own bias into training data without meaning to. So the video asks two questions about any training data: is there enough data? Does it include many kinds of people and situations?

educatorNotes.0.source: The Riverbend test and its numbers (19, 16 and 9 of 20) are made up; the evidence tells learners what the tool learned from, so the cause is given, not worked out from the scores. Real research: Kid-Whisper (Attia and others, AIES 2024) found that Whisper speech models, without extra training, had word error rates 6 to 10 times adults' on scripted children's speech and 3 to 5 times on conversational children's speech in the test sets it used. It names two causes: child speech databases are limited and hard to collect, and children's speech varies as they develop. Training on children's speech reduced errors, and the authors list remaining challenges. Photos: Suresh and Guttag (2021) report that about 45% of ImageNet's 1.2 million labelled images were taken in the United States, 1% in China and 2.1% in India, and cite a study (Shankar and others) finding that a classifier trained on it did significantly worse on images such as “bridegroom” from under-sampled countries like Pakistan or India.
educatorNotes.0.back: The Riverbend test and its numbers (19, 16 and 9 of 20) are fictional. The evidence tells learners what the tool learned from, so it gives the cause; learners do not work it out from the scores. Real research: Kid-Whisper (Attia et al., AIES 2024) found the Whisper speech model without extra training had a word error rate 6 to 10 times higher than adults' for children's scripted speech and 3 to 5 times higher for children's conversational speech, on the test sets used. The study names two causes: children's speech databases are limited and hard to collect, and children's speech changes with development. Training on children's speech reduced errors, and the authors name the challenges that remain. Photos: Suresh and Guttag (2021) report that of ImageNet's 1.2 million labelled images about 45 percent were taken in the US, 1 percent in China and 2.1 percent in India, and cite research (Shankar et al.) finding that classifiers trained on it performed significantly worse on images like “groom” from under-represented countries such as Pakistan or India.
educatorNotes.0.note: word error rate kept in English in brackets after อัตราคำที่ถอดพลาด; classifier = ตัวจำแนกภาพ. Technical terms for adults: check against usual Thai ML usage.

educatorNotes.1.source: Missing examples are one cause of bias, not the only one. Suresh and Guttag list seven sources of harm across the machine-learning life cycle: historical, representation, measurement (how labels are chosen), aggregation, learning (the goal a model is trained for), evaluation (how it is tested) and deployment (how and where it is used). Their heart-attack and hiring examples are a “simplified scenario” they made up to show that the same symptom can have different causes: more data from women helped the first, but not the second, where the labels came from biased human ratings. The lesson says so. A gap in results shows something is wrong, not why. Don't tell learners that bias is always an accident: the lesson says only that a result can be unfair even when nobody planned it. This lesson no longer repeats Lesson 3's model testing; the leaf model and the translation tool were taken out. The claim record is in content/courses/digital-world/claims/DW08.md.
educatorNotes.1.back: Missing examples are one cause of bias, not the only one. Suresh and Guttag name seven sources of harm across the machine learning life cycle: historical, representation, measurement (how labels are chosen), aggregation, learning (the goal the model is trained for), evaluation (how it is tested) and deployment (how and where it is used). The heart-attack and hiring examples are “simplified scenarios” they made up to show that the same symptom can have different causes. More data on women helps the first case but not the second, where labels come from biased human scores; the lesson says this. A gap in results shows something is not right but not why. Do not tell learners bias is always an accident; the lesson only says results can be unfair even if no one planned it. This lesson no longer repeats Lesson 3's model test; the leaf model and translation tool were removed. The claims log is in content/courses/digital-world/claims/DW08.md.
